days.title: Lange und kurze Vokale
goals: Hear and say long vs. short vowels

sections.title: Long or short?
sections.explanation:
German vowels are either **long** or **short**, and length can change meaning: *Staat* [ʃtaːt] (state) vs. *Stadt* [ʃtat] (city). Spanish vowels are all medium length, so this takes practice. In IPA, ː marks a long vowel.

| Spelling | Length | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| vowel + one consonant | long | Tag [taːk], Brot [bʁoːt], Name [ˈnaːmə] |
| doubled vowel | long | Tee [teː] |
| vowel + h (h is silent) | long | zehn [tseːn], wohne [ˈvoːnə], Ihnen [ˈiːnən] |
| ie | long [iː] | Bier [biːɐ̯], vier [fiːɐ̯] |
| vowel + double consonant | short | Mann [man], Wasser [ˈvasɐ], null [nʊl], bitte [ˈbɪtə] |
| vowel + 2 or more consonants | usually short | acht [axt], elf [ɛlf], fünf [fʏnf] |

sections.title: Im Café
sections.text:
– Guten Tag!
– Guten Tag. Ein Wasser und ein Brot, bitte.
– Gern. Und Sie?
– Ein Bier, bitte.
– Das macht zehn Euro.
– Danke!
sections.translation:
– Hello!
– Hello. A water and a bread, please.
– Sure. And you?
– A beer, please.
– That's ten euros.
– Thanks!

items.explanation: One consonant after the vowel → long: [taːk].
Vowel + h → long, and the h is silent: [tseːn].

items.prompt: Match each word to its vowel.

items.explanation: Short a → double s. Nouns are capitalized.

sections.title: Umlauts are their own vowels
sections.explanation:
Umlauts change the word: *schon* [ʃoːn] (already) vs. *schön* [ʃøːn] (beautiful).

| Letter | IPA (long / short) | How to say it | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| ä | [ɛː] / [ɛ] | like Spanish **e** | später [ˈʃpɛːtɐ], Männer [ˈmɛnɐ] |
| ö | [øː] / [œ] | say [eː] / [ɛ], round your lips | schön [ʃøːn], zwölf [tsvœlf] |
| ü | [yː] / [ʏ] | say [iː] / [ɪ], round your lips | Bücher [ˈbyːçɐ], fünf [fʏnf], Tschüss [tʃʏs] |

Many plurals add an umlaut: Mann → Männer, Buch → Bücher. If you can't type them, use ae / oe / ue: the app accepts these but flags them.

sections.title: Lena
sections.text:
Das Mädchen heißt Lena. Lena ist zwölf. Sie hat fünf Bücher. Die Bücher sind schön.
– Tschüss, Lena! Bis später!
sections.translation:
The girl's name is Lena. Lena is twelve. She has five books. The books are beautiful.
– Bye, Lena! See you later!

items.explanation: Say [ɪ], then round your lips without moving your tongue: [fʏnf].

items.prompt: The ä in **später** is closest to Spanish…

sections.prompt:
Read aloud:

**schon – schön, Buch – Bücher, Mann – Männer, fünf, zwölf, Tschüss, später**
sections.modelAnswer: **schön** [ʃøːn], **zwölf** [tsvœlf]: an e with rounded lips. **Bücher** [ˈbyːçɐ], **fünf** [fʏnf], **Tschüss** [tʃʏs]: an i with rounded lips. **Männer** [ˈmɛnɐ], **später** [ˈʃpɛːtɐ]: Spanish e.

sections.title: Vowel pairs
sections.explanation:
| Spelling | IPA | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| ei / ai | [aɪ̯] | nein [naɪ̯n], drei [dʁaɪ̯], Zeit [tsaɪ̯t], heiße [ˈhaɪ̯sə] |
| ie | [iː] | vier [fiːɐ̯], Bier [biːɐ̯], sieben [ˈziːbn̩], Lied [liːt] |
| eu / äu | [ɔʏ̯] | neun [nɔʏ̯n], Freund [fʁɔʏ̯nt], Deutsch [dɔʏ̯tʃ], Häuser [ˈhɔʏ̯zɐ] |
| au | [aʊ̯] | Haus [haʊ̯s], Frau [fʁaʊ̯], aus [aʊ̯s] |

Trick for **ei** vs. **ie**: the *second* letter wins. ei → [aɪ̯] (like Spanish *hay*), ie → [iː].

sections.title: Wie heißt du?
sections.text:
– Wie heißt du?
– Ich heiße Paul. Und du?
– Ich heiße Jose. Ich komme aus Mexiko.
– Freut mich! Mein Freund wohnt in Mexiko.
sections.translation:
– What's your name?
– My name is Paul. And you?
– My name is Jose. I'm from Mexico.
– Nice to meet you! My friend lives in Mexico.

items.explanation: äu = [ɔʏ̯], like eu: [ˈhɔʏ̯zɐ]. The others have au = [aʊ̯].

sections.prompt:
Count aloud: **eins zwei drei vier fünf sechs sieben acht neun zehn**.

Then say: *Wie heißt du? – Ich heiße … Freut mich!*
sections.modelAnswer: eins [aɪ̯ns] – zwei [tsvaɪ̯] – drei [dʁaɪ̯] – vier [fiːɐ̯] – fünf [fʏnf] – sechs [zɛks] – sieben [ˈziːbn̩] – acht [axt] – neun [nɔʏ̯n] – zehn [tseːn]

sections.title: Two ways to say ch
sections.explanation:
| After | IPA | Sound | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| a, o, u, au | [x] | like Spanish **j** (*jamón*) | Nacht [naxt], acht [axt], Buch [buːx], noch [nɔx] |
| everything else | [ç] | like Japanese **ひ** (hi) | ich [ɪç], nicht [nɪçt], Bücher [ˈbyːçɐ], Mädchen [ˈmɛːtçən] |

Never [k] or [ʃ]. Two extras: final **-ig** = [ɪç] (zwanzig [ˈtsvantsɪç]); **chs** = [ks] (sechs [zɛks]).

sections.title: Gute Nacht
sections.text:
– Gute Nacht!
– Gute Nacht! Bis morgen!
Ich lese ein Buch. Das Buch ist gut, aber ich verstehe nicht alles. Ich lerne die Sprache noch.
sections.translation:
– Good night!
– Good night! See you tomorrow!
I'm reading a book. The book is good, but I don't understand everything. I'm still learning the language.

items.explanation: After ü → [ç], even though Buch has [x]: [ˈbyːçɐ].
Standard: [ˈtsvantsɪç]. In southern Germany and Austria you'll also hear [ˈtsvantsɪk].

sections.prompt:
Read the pairs aloud:

**Buch / Bücher – Nacht / Nächte – acht / nicht – noch / ich**

Then: *Entschuldigung, ich verstehe nicht. Noch einmal, bitte.*
sections.modelAnswer: First word of each pair has [x], the second [ç]: Buch [buːx] / Bücher [ˈbyːçɐ] – Nacht [naxt] / Nächte [ˈnɛçtə] – acht [axt] / nicht [nɪçt] – noch [nɔx] / ich [ɪç].

days.title: s, z, sch, sp, st, w, v, j
goals: Remember w = v and v = f

sections.title: Consonants that trick Spanish and English speakers
sections.explanation:
| Spelling | IPA | Note | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| s + vowel | [z] | voiced, as in English *zoo* | Sie [ziː], sieben [ˈziːbn̩], sechs [zɛks] |
| ss, ß | [s] | | Wasser [ˈvasɐ], heiße [ˈhaɪ̯sə], Straße [ˈʃtʁaːsə] |
| z | [ts] | like Japanese つ | zehn [tseːn], zwei [tsvaɪ̯], Zeit [tsaɪ̯t] |
| sch | [ʃ] | | Schule [ˈʃuːlə] |
| sp-, st- at the start of a word or stem | [ʃp], [ʃt] | | Sprache [ˈʃpʁaːxə], Stadt [ʃtat], verstehe [fɛɐ̯ˈʃteːə] |
| tsch | [tʃ] | | Tschüss [tʃʏs], Deutsch [dɔʏ̯tʃ] |
| w | [v] | | Wasser [ˈvasɐ], wohne [ˈvoːnə], wie [viː] |
| v | [f] | in native words | vier [fiːɐ̯], vielen [ˈfiːlən] |
| j | [j] | like Spanish *ya* | ja [jaː] |

ß comes after long vowels and ei/eu (Straße, heiße); ss after short ones (Wasser). Switzerland writes ss everywhere.

sections.title: Wo ist die Schule?
sections.text:
– Entschuldigung, wo ist die Schule?
– Die Schule? Hier, in der Straße, Nummer sieben.
– Vielen Dank!
– Bitte!
sections.translation:
– Excuse me, where is the school?
– The school? Here, on this street, number seven.
– Thank you very much!
– You're welcome!

items.explanation: st at the start of a word = [ʃt]: [ʃtat].
Long [aː] + ß: [ˈʃtʁaːsə]. ('Strasse' is the Swiss spelling.)

sections.title: What happens at the end of a word
sections.explanation:
| Rule | Examples |
|---|---|
| final b / d / g → [p] / [t] / [k] | Tag [taːk], Abend [ˈaːbn̩t], Kind [kɪnt] |
| add an ending → voiced again | Tage [ˈtaːɡə], Kinder [ˈkɪndɐ], Lieder [ˈliːdɐ], Freunde [ˈfʁɔʏ̯ndə] |
| final -er → [ɐ], a short a | Wasser [ˈvasɐ], Männer [ˈmɛnɐ], später [ˈʃpɛːtɐ] |
| vowel + h → long, h silent | zehn [tseːn], wohne [ˈvoːnə], Ihnen [ˈiːnən] |

**r** before a vowel is [ʁ], made in the throat (a soft gargle), never rolled like Spanish rr: Brot [bʁoːt], drei [dʁaɪ̯], Frau [fʁaʊ̯].

words.example: Guten Abend, wie geht es Ihnen?
Guten Tag, Herr Müller! Wie geht es Ihnen?

sections.title: Guten Abend, Frau Weber
sections.text:
– Guten Abend, Frau Weber! Wie geht es Ihnen?
– Gut, danke. Und Ihnen?
– Gut! Mein Kind ist zehn. Es hört jeden Tag Musik.
sections.translation:
– Good evening, Ms. Weber! How are you?
– Fine, thanks. And you?
– Good! My child is ten. He listens to music every day.

items.explanation: With an ending, the d is voiced again: [ˈkɪndɐ].

sections.title: Which syllable is stressed?
sections.explanation:
In IPA, ˈ goes *before* the stressed syllable.

| Pattern | Examples |
|---|---|
| first syllable (default) | Wasser [ˈvasɐ], Sprache [ˈʃpʁaːxə], Name [ˈnaːmə], Kaffee [ˈkafe] |
| after be- / ver- / ent- / ge- | verstehe [fɛɐ̯ˈʃteːə], Entschuldigung [ɛntˈʃʊldɪɡʊŋ] |
| last syllable (many loanwords) | Musik [muˈziːk] |

*Auf Wiedersehen* stresses *Wie*: [aʊ̯f ˈviːdɐˌzeːən]. (Austria often says Kaffee [kaˈfeː].)

words.example: Sprechen Sie Englisch? – Ja, ein bisschen.

sections.title: Ein Gespräch
sections.text:
– Entschuldigung, sprechen Sie Englisch?
– Ja, ein bisschen.
– Danke! Ich spreche ein bisschen Deutsch. Ich heiße Jose und ich komme aus Mexiko.
– Freut mich! Ich heiße Anna Weber.
– Wie bitte? Langsamer, bitte.
– Ich heiße Anna Weber.
– Freut mich! Auf Wiedersehen, Frau Weber!
– Auf Wiedersehen!
sections.translation:
– Excuse me, do you speak English?
– Yes, a little.
– Thanks! I speak a little German. My name is Jose and I'm from Mexico.
– Nice to meet you! My name is Anna Weber.
– Pardon? More slowly, please.
– My name is Anna Weber.
– Nice to meet you! Goodbye, Ms. Weber!
– Goodbye!

items.explanation: Tschüss is casual; Auf Wiedersehen is safe with Sie.

sections.prompt: Write 4–5 lines introducing yourself, using only this week's phrases: a greeting, your name, where you're from, where you live, which languages you speak.
sections.modelAnswer: Guten Tag! Ich heiße Jose. Ich komme aus Mexiko. Ich wohne in Indiana. Ich spreche Spanisch, Englisch und ein bisschen Deutsch.

sections.prompt: **Partner check:** read your introduction to your speaking partner and ask them to correct your pronunciation.
sections.modelAnswer: Ask them to listen for: [x] vs. [ç], [ʏ] / [œ], z = [ts], w = [v], final -er = [ɐ], and stress on the right syllable.

cards.notes: Fine with du and Sie. Unlike Spanish, the H is pronounced.
Final -en is weak: [ən], often [n̩]; r = [ʁ], in the throat: [ˈɡuːtn̩ ˈmɔʁɡn̩].
Neutral-polite, good with Sie. Final g → [k]: [ˈɡuːtn̩ taːk].

Sie-register. Sie: s before vowel = English z.
